claim: Every singleton consonant is attested intervocalically, but root-internal bi- and triconsonantal clusters are restricted to a small set of structural types.
normalized_environment: root-internal medial clusters belong to Dixon types (20a-c)
scope: root-internal clusters; Dixon 1981 as summarized and reanalyzed by Hayes & Wilson
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Many structurally predicted clusters are unattested or occur only once, so structural possibility must be separated from lexical attestation.

claim: The first member of an intervocalic consonant cluster must be a sonorant, and the second member may not be one of the anterior approximants /r, l, ɻ, j/ in the learner's broad generalization.
normalized_environment: C1 in medial cluster => [+son]; C2 != anterior approximant
scope: learned generalization over Dixon vocabulary plus inflected forms
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The weighted grammar allows low-frequency exceptions rather than treating every surface cluster as categorical evidence against the generalization.

claim: Medial cluster phonotactics strongly penalize several heterorganic place combinations, including dorsal-coronal, dorsal-labial and labial-dorsal sequences; the system also favors homorganic nasal-stop sequences.
normalized_environment: avoid selected heterorganic place combinations in medial clusters
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Some nonhomorganic clusters occur, but are sparse; the restrictions are gradient in the learned grammar rather than absolute categorical statements.

claim: Among roughly 2,400 logically possible two- and three-consonant clusters, the learned grammar assigns perfect scores to only 46; this sharply narrows the combinatorial space while still allowing some unattested clusters as predicted accidental gaps.
normalized_environment: cluster well-formedness gradient over logically possible medial clusters
scope: model evaluated against Dixon cluster inventory
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Predicted-perfect but unattested clusters include accidental gaps and analogical projections from attested triconsonantal patterns.

claim: Inflection expands the medial cluster inventory beyond roots, but morpheme-specific alternations often repair clusters so that derived forms reinforce root-internal phonotactics; the ergative/instrumental suffix loses its initial nasal and undergoes place assimilation after nasal-final roots.

source_forms.suffix: -ŋgu after vowels; reduced/assimilated after nasal-final roots

normalized_environment: morphological alternation repairs otherwise expanded medial cluster space
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Some clusters occur only under inflection and therefore genuinely broaden the surface system rather than being repaired away.

claim: Hayes & Wilson identify both accidental gaps and model-sensitive marginal clusters: several legal clusters are unattested, while some attested clusters receive weak penalties because they occur in only one or two roots or only under inflection.
normalized_environment: legal but unattested vs rare attested medial clusters
scope: Dixon vocabulary and inflected learning data
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Hayes & Wilson explicitly warn that corpus frequency can make grammatical but rare clusters look ill-formed to the learner.

claim: The high front vowel /i/ is restricted to prevocalic position and is absent before a consonant or at word end; Dixon's Yotic Deletion removes /i/ in those environments.
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Hayes & Wilson's learner generalizes beyond Dixon and also groups unattested iwC sequences with the iC restriction, which may partly reflect accidental gaps.

claim: Light-syllable words follow an essentially right-to-left trochaic stress pattern, with primary stress on the leftmost stressed syllable.
normalized_environment: right-to-left trochees; primary stress = leftmost stress
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Three-syllable heavy-initial words behave differently because final stress is independently excluded.

claim: A Wargamay syllable is heavy only if it contains a long vowel; heavy syllables are restricted to word-initial position and all heavy syllables bear primary stress.

source_forms.heavy_definition: long vowel; closure does not make a syllable heavy

normalized_environment: heavy iff Vː; heavy => initial and primary stressed
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The description of one five-syllable heavy-initial word is uncertain, so Hayes & Wilson exclude that pattern from further inference.

claim: Polysyllabic Wargamay words do not normally have final stress; three-syllable words beginning with a heavy syllable therefore contain a stress lapse after the initial heavy syllable.
normalized_environment: *final stress in polysyllables; lapse tolerated after initial heavy
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Monosyllables necessarily have final stress; the learned grammar weakly penalizes monosyllabic stress only because such forms are rare in training.
